MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  APRIL 7, 2021

CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee of the City of
Rolling Hills Estates to order at 7:00 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, O’Malley, Radocchio, Schachter, Uppal,
  Wisot, Yoo

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Bacinski, Bain, Chan-Southwell, Larson, Schachter

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Jeannie Naughton, Planning Manager
  Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant

ALSO PRESENT:  Laura Male, Project Manager, Sapphos Environmental
  Jonathan Cain, Sustainability Manager, Sapphos Environmental
  Ryan Johnson, Transportation Planner, Alta Planning

3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING, MARCH 8,
  2021

COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
O’MALLEY to,

  APPROVE THE ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  MARCH 8, 2021

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

NONE

5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A.  WASTE MANAGEMENT RATES AND SERVICE UPDATE (VERBAL)

Assistant City Manager Davis provided background on the City’s contract with Waste
Management which began in 2005. Most recently, there was a significant rate increase for manure
service. Due to the pandemic, Waste Management deferred this rate increase from July 2020 to
December 2020. The City worked with the Subcommittee and consultants to help alleviate the
impact of increased manure service rates and rates for service across the board.
Assistant City Manager Davis provided an overview on the waste and recycling regulations,
through Cal Recycle, that the city must comply with. A new law AB 1383 came into effect, which
requires reducing organics in regular waste, that cities identify edible food recovery programs and
requires that enforcement and penalties measures within the city’s code. The enforcement and
penalties by the State will begin in January 2022. The key legislation of AB 1383 is that, by
January 1, 2022, all jurisdictions must provide organic collection to all residents and businesses.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that what was planned for July 1, 2021 was a CPI
adjustment. An overview of the rate increases, including the manure service, was provided. An
overview of the addition of organic food waste and rates was also presented.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that staff is looking to take this to the City Council on
Tuesday, April 13th for review and approval of an amendment that would implement the organic
waste and the modified rate increase effective July 1, 2021.

CHAIR STEGURA commented that the more you compost of your organic food waste, the less is
put into waste disposal.

COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY asked if there is opportunity for the City to work with the
South Bay Environmental Services to host composting workshops. Assistant City Manager Davis

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, APRIL 7, 2021
 stated that this is a possibility; and, the South Bay Botanic Gardens has composting workshops
as well.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that she attended a composting class at the South Bay
Botanic Gardens and they had bins available for purchase.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that considering where the rates could have gone, this is a good result
and stated that the sub-committee should be commended for their work and thanked Assistant
City Manager Davis for her work as well.

B.  SUSTAINABILITY ELEMENT - POLICY FRAMEWORK/GOAL PRIORITIZATION

Laura Male, Project Manager, Sapphos Environmental stated that they have collected input on
the Sustainability Element from the EAC and GPAC and is currently collecting input from the
community stakeholder groups.

Ms. Male stated that on March 8th, the EAC voted for the following Sustainability Definition:

“Balancing environmental conservation, social responsibility, and economic prosperity to meet
our present needs while ensuring the ability of future generations to meet their needs.”

Ms. Male stated that the discussion tonight will affect three sections of the Sustainability Element,
which are: Section 2.0 – City Sustainability Goals and Existing Policies; Section 4.0 –
Sustainability Element Policies; and, Section 5.0 – Achieving City Goals.

Ms. Male provided a presentation and led the discussion on the City Sustainability Goals and
Existing Policies proposed for the seven sustainability pillars, which include energy, quality of life,
air quality and greenhouse gas emissions, water resources, waste management and recycling,
land use, and mobility.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL asked about energy and if the green building guidelines will be
in place for remodeling or new builds and how they will be enforced. She stated that she is not
sure that anyone really checked if her home remodel project, which was completed two years
ago, met the required green building guidelines.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the City contracts with LA County Building and Safety
and feels confident that if there was a checklist on things that needed to be completed for the
remodel, that those things were checked against the guidelines. LA County has adopted the Cal
Green code which is not as restrictive as it could be. These policies were meant if the City wanted
to be more aspirational and the City would need to work with LA County to have standards that
exceed the Cal Green code and then the County would implement that. The City’s code would
need to be amended to reference the more aspirational requirements. These codes would apply
to any major remodels, complete rebuilds or new construction.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL commented that it would be great to be aspirational for the
energy requirement since it is not difficult to go above and beyond.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that agrees with being aspirational with energy but when a new policy
or code is introduced there is an education period to familiarize themselves with what is being
expected. The energy goals/policies are broad enough to take into account prohibiting the use of
natural gas, which could come down the line.

Jonathan Cain, Sapphos Environmental, encouraged “thinking big” now. There will be further
analysis including the feasibility of implementing the goals and policies.

COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY stated that the standards on a State and Federal level are
changing and it is best to give people awareness so that they take advantage of incentives while
they are being offered.

Ms. Male continued with the goals and policies for quality of life.

COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT stated that noise is an important goal and there should be strict
enough laws to keep noise to a minimum, especially on weekends.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that one thing that will help is an education project to ask landscapers
to use electric blowers that will be rolled out slowly, incentives will be offered to purchase the
tools, and later there would be enforcement.

COMMITTEE MEMBER YOO asked about the biggest contributor to noise pollution.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  2
 MINUTES, APRIL 7, 2021
 COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT stated that it is construction and landscaping.

In response to a question by CHAIR STEGURA, Planning Manager Naughton responded that the
code does not allow for work on Sundays, but the only recourse for construction on Sundays
would be to contact the Sheriff’s Department.

Mr. Cain stated that noise studies could be conducted and a noise monitoring component could
be added. A brief discussion ensued on the feasibility of this.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that the first policy (Goal 4 - Policy 4.1) should be mitigation of noise
verses noise and vibrations studies.
COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL asked in regards to minimizing light pollution (Goal 5 - Policy
5.1), is there is already a code in place for backyard lighting. Planning Manager Naughton stated
that there are provisions in the code that require exterior lights to be cast down and maximum
luminaires called out in the code. In terms of sports court lighting, there are certain hours that
those lights can be on.

Ms. Male continued with the goals and policies for air quality and greenhouse gas emissions.

COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY stated that she works for the South Coast Air Quality
Management District and explained some challenges in creating an air quality monitoring system
and responding to issues that may arise.

COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT asked if it is true that the numbers that are attributed to the City
come from the monitoring station in Long Beach. COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY provided a
brief explanation on how it is determined where the monitoring stations are placed in the region.

A brief discussion ensued on this topic.

CHAIR STEGURA asked if specifically mentioning statutes that may be out code during the life
of the General Plan, specifically as mentioned in Goal 1 – Policy 1.1 – Cooperate with the State
to implement SB32. Mr. Cain stated that the intent of including it would be to show that the City is
demonstrating that it is doing its part to meet the State’s goal, but it could be more broad and take
out the specific legislation. COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY suggested adding “and future
legislation” at the end.

COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO expressed his concern with Policy 1.2 – Lower the
emissions caused by motor vehicles through Transportation Demand management strategies and
land use patterns that reduce vehicle miles traveled and Policy 2.4 – Promote the reduction of
vehicular traffic and improved efficiency of the City’s circulation system (i.e. roadways) as a means
to improving air quality and stated he is not sure if there is anything that can be done with the
roadways, for example Palos Verdes Drive North. COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT stated that he
was on the Traffic and Safety Committee and there is nothing that can be done with Palos Verdes
Drive North.

In response to a question by CHAIR STEGURA, Mr. Cain stated that this does not need be in this
section or it can be less specific.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that this may also include encouraging the walking school bus or using
PV Transit. COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL added that it could also speak to encouraging the
use of electric vehicles.

A brief discussion ensued on the topic of electric vehicles.

Ms. Male continued with goals and policies for water resources.

CHAIR STEGURA expressed concern with requiring people to do things immediately, such as in
Policy 2.4 – Require the installation of… and Policy 2.1 – Implement aggressive…

COMMITTEE MEMBER YOO commented that requiring seems to be mandatory rather than when
it is required to be installed.

In response to a question from CHAIR STEGURA, Mr. Cain stated that 2.4 could be changed to
stated that it is for City facilities.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that with education, there could be simple changes made
to existing sprinkler systems, to make it less onerous.

The Committee agreed to take out the word, “require” and make it more of an education focused
policy.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  3
 MINUTES, APRIL 7, 2021
 Ms. Male continued with goals and policies for waste management and recycling.

Planning Manager Naughton suggested adding partnerships with the South Coast Botanic
Gardens to promote and co-host composting education. CHAIR STEGURA suggested adding
educational efforts with the City’s community partners.

Ms. Male continued with goals and policies for land use.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that in Goal 3 – Policy 3.1 does not mention the use of
pesticides and fertilizers. Mr. Cain stated that there could be a policy created to address this more
specifically.

In response to a question by COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL, Planning Manager Naughton stated
that the contract with the city’s landscape company was amended to prohibit the use of pesticides.
This would be more for residential and commercial throughout the City and maybe provide
outreach and education to discourage the use of pesticides and fertilizers.

Ms. Male continued with goals and policies for mobility.

COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY stated changing from energy efficient vehicles to near zero
and zero emission vehicles (Policy 2.1 and 2.3). The committee agreed.

Ms. Male provided the schedule for the Sustainability Element and provided an update on the
response to the survey and the input map.

Ryan Johnson, Alta Planning, stated that the input map has received 36 suggestions. The general
themes are congestion during certain times of the day, walking and biking gaps were called out,
and safety and speeding. The survey has received 18 responses. Respondents were asked to
rate the seven pillars, land use was on top followed by quality of life and waste management.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the City has posted on their social media pages, staff
also reached out to two PV school Facebook groups, and a reminder will be sent to the City’s
stakeholder list. Staff is open to any suggestions.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL suggested reaching out directly to the schools. Planning
Manager Naughton stated that she reached out to the Deputy Superintendent but has received
no response. Staff will try to reach out to the schools again.

COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY stated that she could post flyers at some of the businesses
frequented by the younger age demographic.

CHAIR STEGURA suggested opening the survey for an additional week. Ms. Male stated that
the new deadline will be April 19, 2021.

Ms. Male provided an overview on the next steps.

6.  CONSULTANT/STAFF ITEMS/COMMITTEE ITEMS

Planning Manager Naughton stated that a new location for an EV charging station and rates will
be brought to the EAC for discussion.

7.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR STEGURA adjourned the meeting at 7:51 p.m.

Submitted by,  Approved by,

_____________________________  ____________________________
Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant  Debby Stegura, Chair
